Okay, you asked why Pankaj didn't talk to me for a week in Class 10. I'm Arnab, and it was my fault.

Pankaj failed the maths pre-board. Before the exam, honestly, none of us knew how he'd do. He'd been studying. He'd done fine in the unit tests. I even told him, "You'll pass easily."

Then the results came out, and in the canteen I said, loud, "Come on, it was obvious. He was always on his phone." Everyone nodded. It felt true when I said it.

Pankaj heard me.

Later that night I remembered my own words, "You'll pass easily." It wasn't obvious at all. I only thought so because I knew the result.

I said sorry the next Monday. He said, "You didn't know either." That stung, because he was right.

qa.q: What did Arnab tell Pankaj before the exam?
qa.a: You'll pass easily.

qa.q: Why did Arnab feel so sure in the canteen that Pankaj's failure was obvious?
qa.a: Arnab felt smug and certain because the result was already known, so it seemed predictable, and saying it felt true in the moment.

qa.q: What could Arnab do next time a friend gets a bad result?
qa.a: Arnab could remember what everyone actually expected beforehand and offer support instead of explaining it as obvious.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel hearing Arnab in the canteen?
qa.a: Pankaj was likely hurt and embarrassed, which is why he stopped talking to Arnab for a week.

grounding: A teenager says a friend's exam failure was obvious, forgetting the earlier prediction that the friend would pass.

Monday, the week before the board practical. Pema watched Vishal set up his circuits in the lab. "You've got this," she told him. Everyone thought he'd do fine; his lab work was usually neat.

Friday. Results were posted. Vishal had failed the practical. His circuit had shorted, and he'd panicked.

That evening, in the group chat, Pema typed, "Honestly it was obvious. He always rushes." Three friends agreed. She felt clever for a moment.

Tuesday, the week after. Vishal came to her desk. "Did you really say it was obvious? You told me I had it."

Pema's face went hot. She remembered Monday clearly now. She hadn't thought it was obvious at all. Nobody had.

"I'm sorry," she said. "I was judging you by what happened, not by what we knew then."

Vishal nodded slowly. "Yeah. That's what it felt like."

qa.q: What did Pema tell Vishal on Monday?
qa.a: You've got this.

qa.q: Why did Pema feel clever for a moment when typing in the group chat?
qa.a: Pema felt clever because, with the result known, the failure seemed predictable, and her friends agreeing made it feel true.

qa.q: What did Pema do well when Vishal confronted her?
qa.a: Pema admitted she had judged by the result rather than what was known before, and apologised directly.

qa.q: How did Vishal feel when he saw the group chat?
qa.a: Vishal likely felt hurt and betrayed, because Pema had encouraged him before and then called his failure obvious.

Elizabeth, you said your friend "obviously" chose the wrong stream? Hmm. Let your Leela aunty tell you something.

When I was sixteen, my best friend Mercy decided to sit the entrance for a nursing school in Chennai instead of doing Class 12 science with me. Everyone thought it was a brave choice. I thought so too. I remember saying, "You'll be brilliant."

She didn't get in. And do you know what I said to the other girls? "It was always a silly idea. Obviously she wasn't ready."

Mercy heard about it. She didn't speak to me for months.

Later I found my old diary. The day she chose, I had written, "Mercy is so brave. I wish I could do that."

I had rewritten my own memory to look wise. That diary taught me: judge the decision by what was known then, not by how it turned out.

So, what did your friend actually know when she chose?

qa.q: What did young Leela write in her diary on the day Mercy chose?
qa.a: Mercy is so brave. I wish I could do that.

qa.q: How did young Leela feel when she found her old diary?
qa.a: Young Leela felt ashamed, seeing that she had rewritten her memory to look wise after Mercy's result.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Leela's story?
qa.a: Finding the diary entry showed that Leela had admired the choice at the time, so calling it obvious later was unfair.

qa.q: How did Mercy feel when she heard what Leela said?
qa.a: Mercy likely felt hurt and betrayed, which is why she didn't speak to Leela for months.

passage:
Dear Rashmi,

I've been thinking about Thursday's review of the rained-out alumni evening. I didn't say enough in the meeting, so I'm saying it here.

Everyone kept saying the risk was obvious: an open-air event in late September. But I went back to our planning notes from July. The weather forecast then said dry. The hall was booked for convocation. The college had held the same event outdoors three years running with no problem. You made the choice with what we knew.

What I heard on Thursday was people judging July with September's information. That's not fair to you.

I'd like to propose that at our next review, we start by asking, "What did we actually know when we decided?" before we talk about what went wrong.

I'm sorry I didn't say this in the room.

Nirmala

qa.q: What did the weather forecast say in July?
qa.a: The weather forecast then said dry.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling after Thursday's review?
qa.a: Nirmala felt uneasy and a bit guilty, feeling the team had judged Rashmi unfairly and that Nirmala hadn't spoken up in the room.

qa.q: What question does Nirmala propose for the next review, and why?
qa.a: Nirmala proposes asking what was actually known when the decision was made, so choices are judged fairly rather than by hindsight.

qa.q: How might Rashmi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Rashmi might feel relieved and supported, knowing someone saw that the choice was reasonable at the time.

grounding: A team member notices colleagues calling a rained-out event's risk obvious and asks what was known when the choice was made.

So you asked about the fest review, Vandana. I'm Farida. Let me tell you what happened in that room.

Our college tech fest lost a lot of money on the celebrity quiz night. Hardly anyone came. In the review, the seniors went straight for Rohit, who'd planned it. "Obviously nobody wanted a quiz on a Saturday night." "Obviously it clashed with the cricket final."

I sat there listening, and something felt off. So I raised my hand. I asked, "When Rohit booked it in January, did anyone know the cricket final would be that day?" Silence. The final was only scheduled in March.

"And did anyone object to Saturday back then?" More silence. We had all voted for it.

I wasn't trying to defend Rohit. I just thought if we're going to learn, we should look at what we knew then.

The mood in the room changed. Rohit looked up for the first time.

qa.a: The final was only scheduled in March.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling as the seniors blamed Rohit?
qa.a: Farida felt uneasy, sensing that something was off about judging the January decision with March's information.

qa.q: Why was Farida's question useful for the team?

qa.q: How did Rohit seem to feel before and after Farida's question?
qa.a: Rohit seemed ashamed and withdrawn during the blame, then relieved when Rohit looked up for the first time.

I'm Yash. I was in the room when our college film club reviewed the screening that went wrong. I'll tell you what I saw.

The projector had failed halfway through, and people had walked out. At the review, everyone said Vaibhav, who organised it, should have known the auditorium projector was unreliable. "It was obvious."

Vaibhav sat very still. Then he took out his phone and read from the booking email. The auditorium staff had written: "Projector serviced last week, fully working." He'd also tested it the day before.

"So what should I have known?" he asked quietly. Nobody answered.

The club president finally said, "Okay. Next time, we ask what we actually knew when we decided." Then she added a backup projector to the checklist.

I don't know what Vaibhav felt exactly. But I noticed he stayed back to help clear up, and he looked a little lighter.

passage:
You asked how I run reviews on my team, Akash. I'm Sumit, and I lead a small sales team at a furniture company. Here's the one habit that changed everything.

Before any big decision, like which city to open in or which client to chase, I write a short note. What we expect to happen. How sure we are. Why we think so. It takes five minutes.

Last year we opened in Nashik. I wrote, "60% chance this works. Main risk: a big competitor might arrive." Six months later, one did, and sales fell.

In the review, one manager said it was obvious we'd fail. I opened the note. "We said 60%. We named this risk. The decision was reasonable. We were unlucky." Nobody got blamed.

But in another case, the note showed we'd ignored a warning. That one, we learned from properly.

Without the notes, everything looks obvious afterwards.

qa.q: What chance of success did Sumit write for opening in Nashik?
qa.a: 60% chance this works.

qa.q: How did Sumit feel when the manager called the Nashik result obvious?
qa.a: Sumit felt calm and confident, because the note showed the decision had been reasonable and the risk was named.

qa.q: Why is writing forecasts before outcomes a fair practice?
qa.a: It shows what was known at the time, so reviews can separate bad luck from bad decisions and avoid wrongly blaming people.

qa.q: How might Sumit's team members feel about this habit?
qa.a: Team members probably feel safer taking reasonable risks, knowing they won't be blamed for bad luck.

grounding: A lead writes forecasts and reasons before decisions so later reviews separate luck from judgement and fewer people are blamed.

passage:
I work on Alka's project team at a publishing house. I'm Rukmini. I don't know everything Alka thinks, but I've watched how she runs things.

Before every book launch, she writes a short sheet: expected sales, how sure she is, and why. She pins it on the board. We all sign it.

Last spring, a travel book we all loved sold badly. At the review, the marketing head started saying, "Anyone could see that cover wouldn't work."

Alka took down the sheet. "In February we all agreed the cover was strong. We said 70% it would sell well. The reason it didn't was a rival book released the same week. We didn't know that."

The marketing head went quiet.

Then Alka asked, "What could we have known?" Someone pointed out that we could have checked other publishers' release dates. We added that to the checklist.

No one was blamed. I remember feeling relieved.

qa.q: What did Alka pin on the board before every book launch?
qa.a: A short sheet: expected sales, how sure she is, and why.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel at the end of the review?
qa.a: Rukmini felt relieved that no one was blamed and the team learned something useful.

qa.q: What did Alka's sheet make possible in the review?
qa.a: The sheet showed what the team knew in February, so the review could separate bad luck from a real gap, like checking rival release dates.

qa.q: How might the marketing head have felt when Alka read the February sheet?
qa.a: The marketing head may have felt caught out and a little embarrassed, having claimed anyone could see the cover wouldn't work.

grounding: A team member watches a lead use written forecasts to review a failed launch fairly, separating luck from judgement.

Monday, early March. Noor, the new team lead at a Bengaluru app studio, started something odd. Before deciding whether to launch a new feature in April, she asked everyone to write down their guess and their reason in a shared file. Jahnavi wrote, "70% users will like it. Reason: beta testers were happy."

Friday, late April. The feature launched. Users hated it. Complaints flooded in. The CEO's first question was, "Who approved this?" Jahnavi felt sick. She'd pushed for it.

Wednesday, early May. At the review, Noor opened the March file. "Here's what we knew. The beta testers were happy. We were 70% sure. What changed was a new phone update that broke the layout. None of us knew that."

The CEO read it twice. "So the decision was sound. The luck was bad."

Jahnavi let out a breath. She hadn't been blamed. And the team added "check upcoming phone updates" to the launch list.

Monday, winter holidays. Jatin opened a new 1000-piece jigsaw of a boring grey bridge. He found it dull after ten minutes. But he'd spent his whole birthday money on it.

Wednesday. Jatin had done the edges. His back hurt. Imran came to call him for cricket. "Two more hours," Jatin said. "I've already done so much."

Saturday. Jatin was still hunched over the grey bridge. Imran came again. "Are you even having fun?"

"No. But if I stop now, all those hours are wasted."

"They're gone anyway," Imran said. "Are the next hours going to be fun?"

Jatin looked at the grey pieces, then out of the window at the sunny street. He slowly put the lid on the box and went to get his bat.

"Come on, Deepak," said his sister Vasudha. "The bus!"

He took another spoonful. Too sweet. His stomach already felt heavy. He took another.

"You don't even like it."

Vasudha sat down. "The money's already spent. Eating it won't bring it back. It'll just make you feel sick and miss the bus."

"Tell Papa thank you," he said, "but I'm full."

Ojas, you're hating that coaching class but you won't quit because of the fees? Let your Joseph uncle tell you something.

When I was fifteen, my parents enrolled me in a medical entrance coaching institute in Kottayam. The fees were huge for our family. By the second year, I knew I hated biology. I wanted to study architecture. I sketched buildings in the margins of my notes.

So I stayed another year. I failed the entrance, of course. Then I finally told my father.

He was quiet for a long time. Then he said, "The fees are gone whether you stay or not. Why did you waste another year?"

I did architecture after that. So, Ojas, what do you want the next year to be for?

It was the week before the mock test, and Nitin's JEE coaching centre was forty minutes away by bus in the pouring rain. He had a fever coming on. He went anyway.

"Why do you keep going?" asked his friend Dolma, sharing an umbrella at the stop. "You hate it. You said you want to do economics."

"Two years, Dolma. My parents have paid for two years. If I quit now, it's all wasted."

"But you're failing the tests."

"I know." He stared at the rain. "Every time I think of quitting, I think of the money. And everyone asking why I gave up."

"And the next two years? If you stay in something you hate, those are wasted too."

Nitin didn't answer. The bus came. He got on, shivering.

That evening, though, he sat down with his parents and said, "Can we talk about economics?"

Kiran had been learning tabla since he was eight. Every Tuesday and Friday, his mother drove him across Pune to Guruji's class. The fees were high; the tabla set had cost a lot.

Now he was fifteen and hated it. He wanted to spend his evenings at the robotics club.

"Why don't you just stop?" asked his sister Damini, watching him drag himself to the car.

"Seven years, Damini. Seven years of classes. Amma bought the tabla. If I stop now, it's all for nothing."

"It's not for nothing. You learned rhythm. You learned discipline. But you're miserable."

Kiran sat in the car, fingers tapping out a rhythm without thinking.

"If you keep going just because of the past," Damini said, "you'll lose the robotics club too."

Kiran was quiet all the way to class. That night, he asked Amma if they could talk after dinner.

College counsellor's note

Parveen, third-year mechanical engineering, came in today. She said she's been unhappy in the course since first year. She wants to study psychology. She's been reading about it in her free time for two years.

When I asked why she hasn't switched, she said, "If I leave now, three years are wasted. My parents will think I threw it all away. I'd be starting over at twenty-one."

I listened. Then I asked her to imagine two versions of herself at twenty-five: one who finished engineering and is still unhappy, and one who switched. She was quiet for a while. She said the second one sounded lighter.

We talked about how the three years aren't erased: she learned maths, problem-solving and persistence.

She's going to talk to her parents this weekend and look at bridging courses. I'll see her again next week.

Hansa

qa.q: What does Parveen want to study instead?

qa.q: Why has Parveen stayed in engineering even though she's unhappy?

Tashi and I have been together since first year. Three years. Everyone thinks we're perfect. And I'm not happy. I haven't been for months.

I'm Chaitanya, and last year I nearly failed the final CA exam for the fourth time.

My parents had spent five years of savings on my coaching. My father told every relative I'd be a chartered accountant. Every time I thought about stopping, I pictured his face at family weddings.

But I hated it. I'd taken a data analyst job to pay for my own books, and I loved that job far more.

My senior at work, Joseph, noticed I looked exhausted. I told him everything. He said, "Your parents invested in you, not in the exam. They'd want you to use that investment well."

So I went home and talked to them. My father was silent for a whole day. Then he said, "We wanted you to be happy. We just thought this was the way."

Career counsellor's note

Keerthana, 24, came to see me today. She is working as a teacher, which she loves. But her parents spent a large sum over three years on coaching for the civil services exam, and she has failed twice.

She told me, "I can't stop. They sold my grandmother's gold for the coaching. If I quit, their sacrifice means nothing." She cried when she said this.

I asked her what she would choose if no money had been spent. She said teaching, without hesitation.

We talked about how her parents' sacrifice was for her future, not for one exam. We practised how she might tell them: thanking them, being honest, explaining what teaching gives her.

She's going home this weekend to have the conversation. I've offered to meet with the family if that would help.

Samir

Neelam's boutique lease was up for renewal on Friday, and she had four days to decide. Her business partner Gopika had already left for a job in Delhi.

For a year, Neelam had poured everything into the little shop in Jaipur: her savings, her evenings, a loan from her uncle. Sales had never picked up.

Every time she thought of closing, she thought, but I've already spent so much.

On Tuesday night, she sat alone among the racks and asked herself one question: if I were starting today, knowing everything I know now, would I open this shop?

The answer came fast. No.

She cried then. For the money, the year, the dream. She let herself grieve it properly.

On Wednesday, she wrote down three things she'd learned: pick a busier street, test demand first, don't rush a partnership.

On Thursday, she called the landlord. She didn't renew. She felt sad, but not ashamed.

Vandana had spent two years preparing for the state civil services exam. Two attempts. Countless evenings in the Nagpur library. Her friend Harsha had watched her grow thinner and quieter.

After the second result, Vandana sat in Harsha's kitchen. "Everyone says try once more. I've already put in so much."

Harsha asked, "If you were starting today, knowing what you know now, would you choose this exam?"

Vandana was quiet for a long time. She thought about the job offer from the NGO she'd been volunteering with, the work she actually loved.

"No," she said. "I wouldn't."

She cried then, for the two years and the plans she'd made. Harsha didn't rush her.

Later, she said, "I learned how to study, how to write, how to keep going. That's not nothing."

The next week, she accepted the NGO offer. She didn't feel ashamed. She felt like she'd finally chosen.

"Jyoti, you've been learning Japanese for a year and a half. Why stop now?"

"Because I asked myself something, Aditi. If I were starting today, would I pick Japanese?"

"And?"

"No. The job I wanted in Tokyo isn't what I want anymore. I love my work here."

"But all those classes. All that money."

"I know." Jyoti's voice wobbled. "I cried about it last night. Eighteen months. I really wanted it."

"So why not finish the course?"

"Because finishing it won't bring back the eighteen months. It'll just take six more."

"That's sad."

"It is sad. I'm letting it be sad. But I'm not ashamed. I learned how to learn a language. I made friends in class. That's not wasted."

"You sound very sure."

"I'm sure about tomorrow. Not about yesterday."

Aditi hugged her. "Okay. Sushi dinner to say goodbye to Japanese?"

"Deal. At least I can read the menu."

Monday, summer holidays. Akash won a shiny blue marble from Zubin. He smiled, put it in his tin, and went back to playing.

Wednesday. Akash lost that same blue marble back to Zubin. He cried so hard his mother came running out. He sulked for the rest of the afternoon and wouldn't eat his mango.

Friday. Zubin sat next to him on the steps. "On Monday you won it, you didn't even jump. On Wednesday you lost it, you cried for an hour. It's the same marble."

Akash sniffed. "Losing it felt way worse."

"Why?"

"Because it was mine."

Zubin held out the blue marble. "Want to play again? Maybe you'll win."

Akash looked at it for a long time. "What if I lose again?"

At the school sports complex, the basketball trial list was pinned to the board. Uday walked past it three times.

Kashish, the chess club captain, noticed. "You're thinking about it, aren't you?"

"Maybe. But I'm the best player in the chess club. If I go to basketball practice on Wednesdays, I'll miss chess, and someone might take my spot."

"You love basketball. You shoot hoops every lunch."

"But what if I'm bad at basketball? Then I'm nobody in either club."

Kashish frowned. "So you'd rather keep the chess spot forever than try something you love?"

Uday stared at the list. Losing his chess rank felt huge, bigger than any possible fun on the court.

"I don't want to lose what I have," he said quietly.

"And what might you gain?" Kashish asked.

Uday didn't have an answer. He walked away without signing.
